channel.description: Tangle's daily edition cut down to Today's topic (the story, what the left and right are saying, and Isaac Saul's take) and Under the radar, plus Isaac's standalone essays. Sponsors, quick hits, extras, teasers, paywalled previews and the Sunday recap are left out.

item.title: The DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit.
item.dc:creator: Isaac Saul
item.description: Could a second Dan Sullivan upend the Senate race?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The DOJ’s Alaska lawsuit. On Thursday, the Justice Department sued Alaska and its Division of Elections director, seeking to preemptively block certification of the state’s Senate election if it is impacted by “voter confusion.” The closely contested race features two candidates named Dan Sullivan; Dan S. Sullivan is the incumbent Republican senator, and Daniel J. Sullivan is a challenger with no party affiliation. The lawsuit alleges that Daniel J. Sullivan entered the race “with the intention of misleading supporters of Senator Sullivan.” Attorneys for Democratic candidate Mary Peltola have asked a judge to dismiss the lawsuit. 

Back up: Alaska uses a top-four primary system, in which the four candidates who receive the most votes (regardless of party) advance to the general election. In this year’s Senate race, former Rep. Peltola (D), Sen. Sullivan (R), Sullivan (no affiliation), and Gerald Heikes (R) advanced to the general election; Peltola and Sen. Sullivan received 49.5% and 41.4% of the primary vote, respectively. The state uses ranked-choice voting for federal and state general elections.

Daniel J. Sullivan, the unaffiliated candidate, is a retired teacher who has not previously held elected office. In May, he announced his candidacy as a Republican, which the Alaska Republican Party challenged. The state’s Division of Elections issued a preliminary finding in June that Sullivan was likely ineligible to run and would be disqualified; however, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled later that month that Sullivan must be included on the primary ballot. To resolve potential confusion over the two candidates, the Division of Elections said the senator should appear with the identifier “(Registered Republican) Incumbent” while the other Sullivan would have “No Party Affiliation.”

The unaffiliated Sullivan has rejected claims that he is running to undermine Sen. Sullivan’s campaign, saying he has long thought about running for office. He has done minimal campaigning, and public records show his campaign has raised negligible funds.

On Friday, President Donald Trump said he directed the Justice Department to file its lawsuit, claiming that Democrats had compelled the second Sullivan to run. The suit similarly argues, “The sole purpose of his candidacy is to benefit the Peltola campaign by reducing the number of votes for Senator Sullivan.” The plaintiffs request that Alaska halt certification until an investigation can determine whether any votes were cast for the wrong candidate.

In their motion to dismiss the suit, Peltola and the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee say the action is part of “a nationwide attack on free elections by the federal government” and “an unprecedented pre-emptive strike on democratic elections.” Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-AK) also questioned the Justice Department’s suit, writing on X, “Alaskans don’t need any help voting for their preferred candidates, and the State of Alaska has already handled this by clearly distinguishing the candidates on this year’s ballot.” 

Today, you’ll read arguments from the right and left about the suit, followed by Executive Editor Isaac Saul’s take.

What the right is saying.
  • Many on the right say the Justice Department is responding properly to manipulative election tactics. 
  • Some suggest the suit is likely to fail. 
  • Others doubt the second Sullivan’s motives, but say he still has a right to run.

The Wall Street Journal editorial board wrote about “exposing ‘Decoy Dan’ in Alaska.”

“Democrats pulled a dirty trick by enlisting a decoy, Daniel J. Sullivan, to run against Republican Alaska Sen. Dan S. Sullivan. Now they are indignant that the Trump Administration on Thursday filed a lawsuit that calls attention to their subterfuge,” the board said. “Democrats deny they are behind the ruse, but their fingerprints are all over it. Daniel J. Sullivan voted for Democrats in the prior three presidential elections and for Democratic nominee Mary Peltola when she ran for the House. There’s evidence that a Democratic consultant also helped launch his campaign.

“Polls show the Senate race within one or two percentage points. That means the election could be decided by a few thousand votes or less,” the board wrote. “Alaska’s convoluted ranked-choice voting system increases the risk of voter confusion. The lawsuit is a legal Hail Mary, but its real purpose before the election is to educate Alaska voters now beginning to pay attention about the Democratic trick. Who’s really undermining trust in elections?”

In Cato at Liberty, Walter Olson argued the suit is “abusive in its intentions.”

“[The suit] borders on frivolous because it attempts to stretch a federal statute, the National Voter Registration Act (NVRA), beyond recognition by snipping language from the law’s preamble and treating it as if it creates vast and open-ended new duties that the federal government can enforce on states,” Olson wrote. “That is not a natural reading of the text, nor is it one that courts have taken. If accepted, it would suddenly federalize many issues of local election administration.”

“It invites suspicions of bad faith by omitting any acknowledgment that Alaska’s printed ballot labels one of the two Sullivans distinctly as ‘incumbent,’ thus helping dispel confusion for a reasonable voter. In so doing, Alaska has addressed the hazard without walking into a different hazard (curbing voter choice by striking an otherwise qualified candidate),” Olson said. “The issue in question is one for the Alaska Supreme Court to decide under Alaska law, and the Alaska court did just that.”

In RedState, Ward Clark said the race “just got more complicated.”

“[The Justice Department] appear[s] to be judging the unknowable intentions of Daniel J. Sullivan in deciding to run for the United States Senate. That’s more or less what the Alaska Division of Elections did last summer, and that didn't work then. I doubt it will work now,” Clark wrote. “I happen to believe that Daniel J. Sullivan did precisely what this lawsuit maintains — he ran as a spoiler, to try to muddy the waters and siphon votes away from the incumbent. But the Alaska Division of Elections can’t read minds, and neither can the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska.”

“There’s a matter of principle here, and the thing about principles is that they must be applied in the same way in every case,” Clark said. “In this case, no matter what we suspect about Daniel J. Sullivan’s motivations (and I'd bet money on them), the only thing that matters here is that Daniel J. Sullivan followed all of the legal procedures and requirements to run for this office. He did so.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left opposes the suit, arguing it was brought too close to the election.
  • Some say the DOJ’s legal arguments are deeply flawed.
  • Others suggest Trump is working to sow doubt about the midterm results.

In Vox, Ian Millhiser wrote “Trump is trying to overturn an election that hasn’t happened yet.” 

“Sen. Sullivan will be identified as a ‘Registered Republican’ and as the ‘Incumbent,’ so voters will be told which Dan Sullivan to vote for if they wish to reelect the one who is actually a senator,” Millhiser said. “Additionally, Alaska uses ranked-choice voting… So an Alaska voter who wants to reelect the Dan Sullivan who is actually a senator, but who is confused as to which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent, can simply rank both Dans Sullivan as their top two choices.”

“Even if Trump’s Justice Department had a persuasive argument that leaving not-Senator Sullivan on the ballot is illegal, they should still lose Alaska because they waited too long to file the case,” Millhiser wrote. “[The Supreme Court has] read this ‘Purcell principle’ quite expansively to forbid federal courts from issuing election-related decisions in the months leading up to an election… If Purcell means anything, it must mean that a federal court cannot force Alaska to kick a candidate off the ballot mere days before a federal election.”

In the Election Law Blog, Rick Hasen argued “the Major Questions Doctrine alone should doom [the suit].”

“[The] DOJ grasps at straws to find some power, any power, contained in a federal statute to give it the authority it demands: to block the certification of a U.S. Senate winner in Alaska until a court can (somehow) investigate possible voter confusion over candidate names,” Hasen said. “The federal government does not even rely upon the part of a law that gives the federal government any power. It instead relies upon some vague statements of purpose of the National Voter Registration Act about the importance of election integrity.”

“Did Congress in the preface to a law about voter registration give DOJ roving power to block state election certification — and presumably other state election processes — in the name of promoting the integrity of the electoral process?” Hasen asked. “The claims to federal power are as ludicrous as they are dangerous. Accepting them would fundamentally change how elections are conducted in America, and shift power away from the states and Congress… to the executive branch.”

In CNN, Aaron Blake said the lawsuit “should raise eyebrows.”

“[The suit signals] a very notable willingness by Trump’s DOJ to engage in highly questionable behavior to try and put its thumb on the electoral scale,” Blake wrote. “[It is] not at all clear how an investigation would ever ascertain how many votes Sen. Sullivan lost due to voter confusion. This issue has already been litigated extensively in court, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that the Daniel J. Sullivan was qualified for the ballot. So this looks like an effort to inject doubt if Peltola wins.”

“And then there’s Trump outright saying he directed his DOJ to file the lawsuit, which carries obvious implications for him politically. That’s not surprising at this point… but it’s still highly problematic,” Blake said. “The 2020 election showed that lawsuits don’t need to succeed to have an impact. Trump’s many wild and false claims of mass voter fraud whipped his supporters into a frenzy… Even absent threats of a violent uprising, these kinds of legal efforts could deliver a pretext for other extraordinary action related to the election.”

My take.
Isaac Saul
Executive Editor
 
 
  • All signs suggest that Daniel J. Sullivan launched his campaign to sow confusion in the election.
  • That doesn’t justify the DOJ preemptively challenging the election results.
  • However, it is another chapter in the ongoing election chicanery both parties have been undertaking for decades, and it’s exhausting.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

President Trump was always going to cast doubt on the results of the 2026 midterms. 

For six years now, I’ve been writing about the various ways the president and his allies have questioned the integrity of our elections. And when they lose (or expect to lose) races they care about, those questions evolve into outright challenges. 

The president refused to accept the 2020 election results when he lost, and he even refused to accept the margins by which he won elections in 2016 and 2024. It’s equally likely he will not accept whatever happens to his preferred candidate in 2028, presuming he doesn’t attempt to find a legal pathway to a third term (and I don’t think he will).

So I wasn’t exactly surprised to see the Department of Justice announce its preemptive lawsuit about the results in Alaska. Nor was I surprised to see Trump say openly that he had instructed the DOJ to file the lawsuit, a confession that would have been a monthslong scandal in any other administration. And yet…

And yet. 

The situation in Alaska is quite preposterous.

Over the summer, The New York Times sent a reporter to meet “candidate” Daniel J. Sullivan, and it discovered the following: Daniel J. Sullivan has never before run for office. He has voted for the Democratic candidate in the last three presidential elections and has never voted for Sen. Dan Sullivan, the Republican incumbent he’s running against. He attends “No Kings” protests and is politically active against the Trump administration.

Despite that, he registered as a Republican just two days before he filed to run in the Senate race. Later, when corresponding with the Division of Elections about his candidacy, he gave his name as “Dan S. Sullivan,” despite his middle name starting with a “J” (Sen. Sullivan’s middle name just happens to start with an “S”). He chalked this up to a “typo,” even though the “J” and “S” are on opposite sides of the keyboard (if it were actually a typo, I’ll leave it to you to decide what kind of galactic coincidence it is that the typo produced an “S”).

On his campaign website, the challenging Sullivan uses a similar Alaskan flag theme as the Republican incumbent, with the same color schemes and stars. Yet, on Daniel J. Sullivan’s website, there are no policy positions outlined. 

He is not campaigning. 

He is hardly raising money. 

He doesn’t seem to be trying to win at all. 

So: Does anyone actually think this is anything but an attempt to undermine Sen. Dan S. Sullivan? I don’t see any reason to pretend. Daniel J. Sullivan hired the longtime Democratic consultant Amber Lee to help him file (again, as a Republican — and again, with the same name as the sitting Republican senator). When asked about this by The Times, he demurred, saying he didn’t want to talk about it because of ongoing litigation. He conceded that he figured his name would offer “an instant megaphone” for his campaign, though he hasn’t used that megaphone to do much campaigning, if any. The duplicitous candidate has played coy, but his intentions seem transparent. 

Now: How big of an impact will this have on the election? My guess is very, very little. This is a ranked-choice election, so Daniel J. Sullivan is likely to be eliminated after the first round (assuming no candidate gets to 50% immediately). Even in an election where only a few hundred thousand people will cast votes, I have a hard time imagining a scenario where the challenging Sullivan will make a big difference. I’m also happy to cede that only the least informed voters here will get confused, and even then they can still simply vote for both Sullivans. Kudos to Alaska’s election officials, who — recognizing they can’t remove Daniel J. Sullivan from the ballot — have done a great job making sure everyone knows who is who:

None of this adds up to an election that has been compromised, or an election whose results are preemptively corrupted. The DOJ insisting an election result not be certified before the election takes place, in the event its preferred candidate loses by a certain number of votes, is ludicrous and dangerous. The annoying truth is that there may actually be some genuine Daniel J. Sullivan voters out there. Every election has protest votes (my dad is a poll worker in Pennsylvania, and he has to stay late counting ballots for Mickey Mouse and Donald Duck every year). If Republicans and Democrats can’t win a vote from disaffected Alaskans over a pretend candidate like this, that’s more a party problem than a Daniel J. Sullivan problem.

And yet.

I can’t focus all my ire on the Trump administration. I have plenty to spare for Daniel J. Sullivan, who is clearly trying to siphon votes from the Republican Party and upend the already sensitive ranked-choice voting election in Alaska.

To be honest, I’m exhausted by these dirty tricks and the partisans who defend them. In Texas, right-wing activists generated a totally made-up “mental health crisis” story about James Talarico and seemed to send out fliers and texts pretending to be trans organizations. All the while, they’ve run AI-generated ads of Talarico scribbling notes in a Bible and reading made-up passages. They do this instead of honestly campaigning on the issues or promoting their candidate to the electorate. Republicans and Democrats are both running fake news websites boosting their own candidates. Republicans and Democrats are both putting money into the other party’s primaries to fund candidates they think they’ll beat in a general election, rather than spending on their preferred candidates. 

It goes on and on and on like this — cheap, dirty, lame political plays from people who can’t win with an affirmative message about what they’ll do. And that’s to say nothing of the gerrymandering or robocalls or vicious and desperate personal attack ads permeating this year’s midterms. 

So, do I worry about the Trump administration preemptively challenging an election result before election day? Of course. I’m gearing up for a long, arduous, infuriating post-election series of denials and conspiracy theories that I’ll have to write about here. But also, in this specific case, I think Republicans’ frustration is warranted. In fact, I blame Daniel J. Sullivan for giving Trump a politically defensible reason for challenging the election results. Democrats would be just as mad, and probably just as litigious, if a Republican voter with the same name as their incumbent candidate got on the ballot as a Democrat with the help of a Republican operative in a competitive Senate race while not actually campaigning, running on any specific issues, or even trying to win.

For all of that, Daniel J. Sullivan — like election deniers and political tricksters trying to corrupt an otherwise functioning electoral system — deserves our scorn. 

Staff concurrence.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
I’m in lockstep with Isaac on the second Sullivan — I believe he’s a sham candidate who entered the race to sabotage Sen. Sullivan. And yet… the DOJ’s lawsuit concerns me more.
 
RedState’s Ward Clark is an unabashedly pro-Trump commentator, but I thought he made the most principled point against the DOJ’s lawsuit of all the writers we surveyed today: “No matter what we suspect about Daniel J. Sullivan’s motivations… the only thing that matters here is that Daniel J. Sullivan followed all of the legal procedures and requirements to run for this office.”
 
More specifically, Republicans challenged the unaffiliated Sullivan’s candidacy, and the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he qualified for the ballot. In that case, what grounds does the Justice Department have to bring a preemptive suit? Cato’s Walter Olson and the Election Law Blog’s Rick Hasen both noted that the DOJ’s reading of the National Voter Registration Act assumes the federal government has the power to interfere with states’ certification of their elections (and possibly other state election processes). It’s a tortured interpretation of the law, and one that, if affirmed, would dissolve the constitutional boundary between federal and state governments in administering elections.
 
Fortunately, I don’t think the lawsuit will succeed. But even as I share Isaac’s (and Republicans’) frustration with what’s playing out in Alaska’s Senate race, I’m much more alarmed by the power the DOJ seeks to assert in its response.

Take the survey: What do you think of Sullivan’s candidacy and the DOJ suit? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The Ohio attack ad.
item.dc:creator: Audrey Moorehead
item.description: Plus, an under-the-radar story about fake polls.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

Editor’s note: Today’s edition contains references to sexual assault.

Vivek Ramaswamy’s attack ad. On Tuesday, Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy’s (R) campaign released an advertisement featuring his opponent Amy Acton’s (D) mother, Donna Arthur, accusing her daughter of lying about her childhood and urging Ohioans to vote against her. The ad has generated backlash after Acton’s campaign and news outlets highlighted that Acton’s stepfather, whom Arthur remained married to until his death, was charged with sexually assaulting Acton when she was 12. 

Ramaswamy and Acton are running to replace outgoing Gov. Mike DeWine (R). Ramaswamy is an entrepreneur and ran for president in 2024; Acton is a physician and previously served as the director of the Ohio Department of Health. Most polls show Acton with a narrow lead, and Sabato’s Crystal Ball rates the race as a toss-up.

Back up: In 1978, Cledith Arthur was charged with sexually assaulting Acton, his stepdaughter. After he was indicted, he fled Ohio with Acton’s mother; they never returned, and he died in 2004. Acton and her mother have not been in contact since 1978. 

On Tuesday night, Ramaswamy’s campaign confirmed it had produced the advertisement and plans to spend $4 million to air it in Ohio. “This is a campaign-ending moment for Amy Acton. The people who know her best keep warning Ohioans about her,” campaign manager Jonathan Ewing said. 

In a statement shared by Acton’s campaign, her brother, Philip Stearns, said, “After he was arrested and Amy and I were removed from their custody, our birth mother stayed married to Amy’s rapist until he died. This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core.” In her own statement, Acton said, “Between the ages of 10 and 12, I was sexually abused by her husband, while my birth mother did nothing to protect me. I’ve always known that she was deeply sick and unwell, and it’s sad to see Vivek Ramaswamy exploit her all for his own political gain.” 

Democrats and some Republicans, including Gov. DeWine, have criticized the ad in light of revelations about Acton’s mother, calling for the Ramaswamy campaign to pull it from the air. However, on Wednesday, Vice President JD Vance said he was “a little bit disgusted” to see Republicans “whining more about that advertisement than they are about what the congressional Democrats and other Democrats want to do to the United States of America.” 

Below are views from the left and right on the ad and how it could affect the race. Then, Editor Audrey Moorehead’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left criticizes the ad and its exploitation of a sensitive family issue.
  • Many say the episode reflects poorly on Ramaswamy. 
  • Others suggest that leveraging family conflict rarely benefits campaigns.

In Slate, Ian Prasad Philbrick said the campaign reached “new depths of depravity.”

“It’s an ugly day in Ohio politics… A mysterious new ad features Acton’s estranged mother, who sided with Acton’s stepfather after she accused him of molesting her,” Philbrick wrote. “Earlier this year, [Ramaswamy] described his candidacy as a chance to elect a governor with ‘a positive vision for our state versus a governor who has none at all other than to complain about what someone else did to her’ — a remark some have read as blaming Acton for her own alleged abuse.”

“This isn’t the first time Arthur has disputed her daughter’s claims… But even Arthur’s version of events does confirm that Acton accused her stepfather of rape, that a grand jury investigated it, and that Arthur visited court ‘to support her husband,’” Philbrick said. “At the very least, the ad is a slimy attempt to weaponize a family dispute. If Acton’s accusations are true, then the ad provides a platform to someone who sided with Acton’s abuser — while also attempting to leverage that abuse for political gain.”

In The Columbus Dispatch, Ray Marcano suggested the ad “will reflect worse on [Ramaswamy] than on Acton.”

“Political operations show desperation when they go from the gutter and venture deep into the muck,” Marcano wrote. “One thing’s clear: Ramaswamy’s campaign should denounce an ad that reaches a new low, but it won’t because, at least for a little while, people will talk about it, and it will force Acton to address it (and she should). But then, the other shoe will drop… Why would a mother attack her daughter in such a public way? Who’s behind the video? Was she paid to appear? Why did she stay with the man who sexually abused a preteen?”

“There will be stories about the recklessness and wretchedness of GOP operatives and how Ramaswamy’s team all but cosigned the latest smear attempt that will reflect worse on him than on Acton,” Marcano said. “The October surprise could sting Ramaswamy instead, as voters wonder why a man who touts integrity lives in a campaign of lies. The hunger for power often leads to the muck. That’s where we are. It’s not a place that’s going to help the GOP.”

In Newsweek, Shane Croucher called the ad “loser behavior.”

“If the morality of the ad isn’t giving Ramaswamy and his team second thoughts, perhaps its real-world political value should, if history is anything to go by,” Croucher wrote. “A Newsweek review of House, Senate and governors’ races found 13 cases, across 12 contests going back to 2000, in which one side used the other candidate's relatives against them: estranged and former spouses, siblings, an aunt, a cousin and now a mother.

“The outcomes are more instructive than the ads. In the 10 cases where the votes have been counted, the side that reached for the family lost seven times. If this was Ramaswamy's Hail Mary, the early evidence says it is being picked off,” Croucher said. “The proof is in the pudding. If polls taken after the ad show Ramaswamy gaining, especially among the independents Marist found breaking for Acton, it will have worked, despite the disgust among many observers.”

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some calling the ad morally indefensible.
  • Others criticize Ramaswamy’s campaign for focusing on non-substantive issues.
  • Still others say the ad’s critics are hypocrites.

In National Review, Kathryn Jean Lopez argued it “is inappropriate content for a political ad.”

“It’s likely to backfire, and it should. It’s amoral and should be a political disaster,” Lopez wrote. “I saw the pro-Vivek ad with Amy Acton’s estranged mother this morning and did what I imagine a lot of people did — looked up who Donna Arthur is and what the backstory is. Acton refers to herself as a childhood sexual-abuse survivor and has talked about being homeless (including in a campaign ad of her own). Her life story includes family-court battles.” 

“Common decency should dictate this being off-limits as a line of attack in a political campaign,” Lopez said. “I see all kinds of questioning of the record online. [Acton’s] positions and political record should be enough to challenge her. If political battle can’t be waged within those limits, the competency of your campaign should be in question... October is known for disgusting political attacks, but we cannot be indifferent or tolerant — this must be condemned.”

In The Daily Caller, Adriel Gonzalez wrote “some campaigns would rather air dirty laundry than make their case.”

“Campaigns have decided embarrassing an opponent is easier than making a convincing case against them — and we’re worse off for it,” Gonzalez wrote. “What campaigns increasingly skip is the harder part — explaining why any of the personal jabs matter to the job their opponents are asking voters to let them do… A new ad targeting Dr. Amy Acton in Ohio is a near-perfect case study in the difference between an attack that generates attention and one that gives voters a meaningful reason to reject a candidate.”

“If the goal is to convince Ohioans to vote for Ramaswamy — or at least against Acton — forcing voters to untangle an ugly family dispute is a bizarre way to make the case,” Gonzalez said. “At the end of the day, there’s a difference between exposing something voters should know and exploiting something people will gawk at. We deserve better than to have spectacle passed off as substance.”

In PJ Media, Matt Margolis said the outrage “exposes a blatant double standard.”

“Democrats have discovered a convenient new rule of political combat. A candidate’s family, they now insist, is strictly off-limits, and anyone who drags a relative into a campaign has sunk to a shameful new low. You’ll notice the rule seems to apply only when a Democrat is in the crosshairs,” Margolis wrote. “I don’t know anything about Acton's family history, and I won’t pretend to… What I can say is that the faux outrage from the left over using a candidate’s mother in an attack is peak hypocrisy.” 

“There’s definitely a legitimate debate over such a tactic. Still, the left is hardly in a position to be claiming some moral high ground on the issue, because using family to attack a political rival is a pastime of the Democrat Party, and the receipts are easy to find,” Margolis said. “Democrats never objected to this playbook when it served their purposes. Democrats have spent years turning candidates’ own families against them and forfeited any claim to the moral high ground long ago.”

My take.
Audrey Moorehead
Editor
 
 
  • I find any attack ad using a candidate’s family in poor taste, even if such ads are common.
  • This particular ad, however, is egregious; it’s cold and Machiavellian at best and cruel and vindictive at worst.
  • Ramaswamy is doing more to indict his own character than Acton’s.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Alone in a vacuum, Vivek Ramaswamy’s new ad isn’t uniquely offensive.

In the ad, Amy Acton’s mother sits in a room and somberly tells the camera that she loves her daughter, “but when I saw her lying about her opponent — it’s not easy for a mother to say this — but Amy has a serious problem.” She says Amy has lied about her past and is unfit to serve as Ohio’s governor. She also substantiates her perspective by mentioning her own history, including working on sexual abuse programs in Ohio.

Don’t get me wrong, the ad is nasty and shocking. The idea that a candidate’s mother might oppose their own kid has a way of stopping you in your tracks. And the specific attacks Donna Arthur levels against her daughter are personal; it’s not “Amy’s platform is bad” or “Amy has supported bad policies” but “Amy is a liar.”

It doesn’t sit well with me for one family member to oppose another in a political race, at least in a public attack ad that’s going to air on TV. But despite my taste, I know that using an opponent’s family members in a political attack ad isn’t really anything new. In 2018, The Washington Post catalogued four politicians whose family members had publicly denounced them, either in ads or online; some of these attacks were personal, like the police officer brother of Democratic candidate Randy Bryce highlighting Bryce’s old tweet comparing law enforcement officers to terrorists (and Randy Bryce’s campaign then released a letter from the men’s mother, exacerbating the personal conflicts). As right-wing commentators like Ben Shapiro and Matt Margolis (under “What the right is saying”) are keen to point out, Democrats have not been shy about boosting their opponents’ liberal family members — from the Kennedys to Mary Trump — as they publicly denounce their relatives. It’s an unfortunate fact of our political culture that attack ads get personal; so, in that context, I mostly resigned myself to the ad’s existence.

But Acton’s campaign’s response casts the ad in a whole new light. Acton and her brother each shared that they are estranged from their mother because, when Amy Acton was 12, her mother’s husband was charged with raping her. Donna Arthur then skipped town with her husband after he was indicted for the crime. Court records and a resurfaced 2020 interview with Arthur appear to support Acton’s brother’s version of events. Arthur’s best defense in 2020 was to say “my daughter lied and said my second husband had raped her”; and Arthur admits to leaving town to avoid the heat. She claims in the interview that charges against her husband were dropped but supplies no evidence for her claim; instead, the case appears never to have been resolved after Arthur and her husband fled. All in all, the full picture of Donna Arthur is of a much less trustworthy source than the ad leads an unsuspecting viewer to believe.

When I rewatch the ad after understanding the full context, it evolves from nasty to outright chilling. That Donna Arthur begins the ad by listing her experience developing sexual assault programs feels like a slap in the face. The accusation that her daughter is a liar goes from just personal to plainly vindictive. One stops seeing the ad as “concerned mother speaking out” and starts seeing it as “angry mother lashing out,” and then one ends up wondering, who the heck approved this?

Unsurprisingly, the backlash to the ad has been fierce. Commentators have circled in on the amoral absurdity of using the woman accused of directly contributing to Acton’s childhood trauma in a political attack. At best, the ad is ruthless and insensitive, a product of pure, Machiavellian calculation; at worst, the ad is directly cruel, weaponizing a woman who protected Acton’s alleged abuser in a way that goes beyond political gamesmanship.

The ad initially featured none of the usual, legally required credits for funding, and it hadn’t actually aired anywhere when an Ohio-based political X account posted it online. It was picked up quickly by right-wing influencers, and initially it wasn’t clear if it came directly from the Ramaswamy campaign, which didn’t confirm or deny its involvement. At first, I expected the campaign to quietly distance itself from the ad. I wondered if it was a gamble that had been leaked online to test the waters, and now that the backlash proved the gamble to be a bad bet, it would soon disappear from Ramaswamy’s campaigning. Instead, in the past few days, he has doubled down: He defended the ad, claimed Acton wouldn’t debate him, and argued that Arthur’s lack of support for Acton is “part of a pattern” that proves she isn’t a trustworthy candidate. Then, news outlets reported that Ramaswamy would spend $4 million to air the ad on TV statewide.

Given all this, I’m left with a thoroughly sour taste in my mouth, not unlike the taste I’ve been left with regarding Graham Platner or Max Miller. To be clear, producing a nasty political attack ad is an order of magnitude less severe than abuse or sexual assault itself. It’s cruel and inappropriate, but it’s not on the level of doing another person physical harm. Nevertheless, it reveals a deficiency of character to dig into a person’s history and find their estranged mother to weaponize against them; to see the shocked, outraged reactions it generates and double down is beyond the pale. 

Again, under the best possible explanation, Ramaswamy is trying to win this election by any means necessary. Political ruthlessness isn’t an uncommon tactic, especially in a political landscape dominated by Trump’s shadow; the president’s personal vendettas against enemies haven’t stopped him from returning to the White House and have even gained him support in the past. But are the payoffs of that sort of ruthlessness really worth debasing yourself morally? And, not for nothing, the strategies that worked for Trump haven’t always been replicable, and the backlash Ramaswamy has received could portend a total backfire. Rather than dealing the Acton campaign a finishing blow, it seems like Ramaswamy has handed her a new weapon to use against him, enabling her to cast him as an amoral power-seeker.

I find myself thinking about this in relation to the trials Ramaswamy has faced in his own political career. It’s no secret that Ramaswamy has faced severe discrimination as the GOP gubernatorial candidate over his religion and his race; his earnest appeals to commonalities between Hindus and Christians have fallen on the mocking ears of the “Groyper” right. 

Ramaswamy’s race and religion have nothing to do with his fitness to be the governor of Ohio. Claims that say otherwise are indefensible. But in the same vein, I would expect him to understand that Amy Acton doesn’t deserve to be attacked for unspeakable things she endured in her childhood. Instead, Ramaswamy is dragging the worst parts of her life into the spotlight, under the flimsy pretense that it’s her character he’s attacking. But now, it seems clear that the ad has backfired, and that it says far more about Ramaswamy’s character than Acton’s.

Staff concurrence.
Russell Nystrom
Associate Editor
 
 
It’s not every day that we can universally recognize a wrong in our increasingly partisan landscape. But we sure came close with this one.
 
While most Republicans were mum on the ad, preferring not to wade into potentially troubled waters, those who did speak were nearly universal in their criticism: Nikki Haley called Ramaswamy a “bad guy,” Rep. Nancy Mace (SC) called it the most “shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season.” Even Sen. Jon Husted (OH), who is on the same ballot as Ramaswamy, said he wouldn’t have run the ad. But there was one exception: Vice President JD Vance defended the ad during his campaign trip to Ohio yesterday, saying “Vivek Ramaswamy had the audacity to run a TV commercial which calls it out like it is and calls Amy Acton a liar.”
 
Not only did Vance prioritize an ad that tested well with “persuadable voters” over basic human decency, but doing so was also a strategic blunder. When that ad was being universally panned, Vance should have read the tea leaves and joined the chorus distancing themselves from it. Instead, he doubled down, making Republicans look even worse and further nationalizing an issue that he and the rest of the party could have taken the high road on.

Take the survey: What do you think of the ad? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

Under the radar.

On Tuesday, a group called Wedgewood Polls released a statement saying that it had fabricated its findings as part of an “experimental project” to highlight vulnerabilities in the political polling industry. Political news site FiftyPlusOne said that the announcement came after they reached out to Wedgewood to inquire about its methodology and leadership. FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, Nate Silver and others had reported results from Wedgewood’s polls, which appeared to mostly favor Democratic candidates. The news marks the second incident in the 2025-26 election cycle of a firm admitting to fabricating poll results. Axios has the story.

item.title: The U.S.–Ukraine policy shift.
item.dc:creator: Will Kaback
item.description: Plus, has Russia expanded its war efforts in the past year?
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The U.S.–Ukraine relationship. On Wednesday, October 14, Ukrainian officials reported that its access to the services it uses to coordinate drone missions was hampered, signaling a potential shift in U.S. policy toward the country amid its war with Russia. The disruption came on the heels of a deal to buy Russian diesel, an executive order lifting sanctions passed by Congress in September, and comments from President Donald Trump accusing Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky of not wanting to end the war. 

Ukraine uses SpaceX Starshield, an upgraded military version of its Starlink satellite internet service, to power both its offensive and defensive drone operations. Although Ukraine reported its connectivity was restored on Thursday, President Zelensky said that the speed of its connection was still degraded over the weekend. “We lose both drones and connectivity,” he said.

Both President Trump and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk deny involvement in Ukraine’s disconnection. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the U.S. military and ultimately [the president],” Musk wrote on X. Meanwhile, Trump stated, “I don’t know if it was anybody because it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” adding that “from what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.” 

Reporting since then has cited anonymous sources who contradict those statements. On Thursday, citing “two U.S. officials and one Western official,” Reuters reported that the order to throttle Ukraine’s Starshield service came from the White House. Then on Friday, The Telegraph reported that Musk approached Trump about shutting off the service and that the Trump administration had warned Ukraine that it could do so if the country didn’t stop its campaign of bombing Russian oil infrastructure. The Wall Street Journal reported on Tuesday that Musk ordered the slowdown. 

On Monday, President Trump appeared to absolve Russia of its recent strikes. “Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine” and “they haven’t been doing much,” Trump said. Later on Monday, Zelensky said that Russia hit Ukraine with missile and drone strikes overnight with “no warning from our partners.” 

Secretary of State Marco Rubio stressed that the U.S. was not seeking to deliberately harm Ukraine, further denying that the White House restricted its Starshield access. Rubio took a 45-minute call with Zelensky on Tuesday, ahead of a round of peace talks with White House envoy Steve Witkoff aimed at presenting Putin with a peace deal. “No doubt there are tensions,” Rubio said. “That is why we had the call.”

Below, we’ll get into what the right and left are saying about the latest with Ukraine and the United States. Then, Senior Editor Will Kaback gives his take.

What the right is saying.
  • The right is mixed, with some criticizing the Trump administration for the Starshield slowdown.
  • Some say a U.S. summit with Russia and China would sow division among the GOP.
  • Others support Trump’s response to Zelensky’s actions.

In National Review, Dan McLaughlin argued “there are no good answers” for Ukraine’s cut-off defense shield. 

“The latest fiasco from the Trump administration involves the apparently deliberate outage of the Starshield system that assists the defense of Ukraine from Russia’s war. This is, rightly, a major national security scandal,” McLaughlin wrote. “Whatever this is, it’s neither responsible behavior nor good domestic politics, which is why nobody is claiming responsibility… There has been surprisingly little effort put into denying that this happened or constructing any counternarrative.”

“If the decision came from the Trump White House, either at the direction of the president or of his political operatives, it is likeliest that it was done for reasons of politics, statecraft, or some murky and self-convinced combination of the two… In any event, simple stonewalling seems unlikely to work,” McLaughlin said. “A bipartisan group of nine senators… have called for an investigation. Pretending that this is going away will not be an option.”

The New York Post editorial board said a summit with Russia and China would “blow up the Republican Party.”

“If President Donald Trump wants a full-on riot within the Republican Party, going along with Vladimir Putin’s idea for a ‘Yalta 2’ summit with Xi Jinping is the way to do it,” the board wrote. “[The 1945 Yalta Conference between the U.S., Britain, and Soviet Union] was a meeting of allies — this new one would be Trump volunteering to be outnumbered by our determined foes… Yet the biggest problems start long before any sitdown. 

“However much Trump thinks he can work with Xi, however charmed he is by Putin, doesn’t matter: Simply announcing he means to do this would instantly prompt all-out rebellion by much of the GOP, further sinking the party’s chances in the midterms,” the board said. “For all Trump’s desire to end the carnage in Ukraine, this won’t do it: Putin’s looking to win via diplomacy what he can’t on the battlefield, and would be happy to see it destroy Trump’s presidency as an added bonus.”

In PJ Media, Scott Pinsker suggested “Zelensky doesn’t have the cards.”

“According to Volodymyr Zelensky, President Donald Trump has joined Russia’s side — and now our partnership is over,” Pinsker wrote. “Foreign policy disputes are seldom singular; this one is no exception. There’s the sky-high casualty count on both sides, the risk of escalation, and Russia’s nuclear arsenal. But the recent finger-pointing has to do with President Trump wanting to purchase Russian diesel fuel — and Ukraine targeting Russian refineries with American weapons, intelligence, and military assistance.”

“It’s obvious why Ukraine is attacking Russian refineries: Kill the Russian economy, and you kill the Russian war machine… It’s equally obvious why President Trump vehemently opposes the idea: American workers and American farmers need diesel,” Pinsker said. “Zelensky isn’t an angel, and he isn’t a demon. He’s a Ukrainian nationalist. He has his national interests — and so do we… He wants America’s interests to align with Ukraine’s, and not the other way around. It’s the exact wrong strategy at the exact wrong time.”

What the left is saying.
  • The left says Trump’s actions show clear favor for Russia.
  • Some suggest a summit with Putin would yield bad results for Ukraine and Trump.
  • Others argue that Ukraine should have control over its future.

In The New Yorker, Susan B. Glasser called Trump’s recent actions a “pivot to Putin.”

“[Trump] finally decided to begin openly helping Vladimir Putin in Russia’s war of conquest against Ukraine,” Glasser wrote. “The latest twist in Trump’s years-long flirtation with outright support of the Russian war effort began last Friday, after the President held a lengthy call with Putin and announced that he was waiving energy sanctions on Russia to purchase hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel fuel — in an attempt… to bring down surging prices.”

“He began a drumbeat of accusations against Zelensky, blaming him and not Russia for the ongoing war, demanding that Ukraine stop attacking Russian energy facilities, and even calling for the Ukrainian President’s ouster,” Glasser said. “After U.S.-supplied Starlink satellite service temporarily went down in advance of another large-scale Russian attack, Zelensky spoke publicly of the rift as all but a permanent break… Demanding that Ukraine fire Zelensky is hardly the rallying cry that Americans are looking for in this season of our own discontent.”

In Slate, Fred Kaplan argued the summit “won’t go well for Trump — or for Ukraine.”

“Zelensky recently admitted that if Trump proceeds on this course, if the United States officially allies with Russia in this war, Ukraine cannot possibly win,” Kaplan wrote. “And all this — Putin’s proposal for a summit, Trump’s waiver of anti-Russia sanctions, and… the severe limiting of Elon Musk’s satellite feeds to Ukraine — comes at a time when Ukraine had been making some headway in the war and Russia had been suffering enormous setbacks… The question at the moment is this: Will Trump actually agree to attend this summit?”

“The lambasting that Trump has received for his diesel-fuel deal and his waiver of Russian sanctions — not only from almost all Democrats but from many Republicans — may have surprised him, and given him a taste of the outrage he’d incite by taking another step toward full appeasement of Putin,” Kaplan said. “We can hope, but, as the saying goes, hope is not a strategy — nor can it offer any insight into how Trump might weigh his desperation for recognition as a powerful leader against the consequences of abandoning Ukraine.”

The Guardian editorial board criticized “diplomacy of the strong for the strong.”

“Does Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump?” the board asked. “The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr. Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr. Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. 

“Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr. Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men,” the board said. “Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal.”

My take.
Will Kaback
Senior Editor
 
 
  • Supporting Ukraine has obvious short- and long-term benefits, and I’m highly alarmed that the White House doesn’t seem to appreciate that.
  • Warming up to Putin doesn’t help us — even at the pump.
  • I can only hope Trump will reverse course as he’s done in the past; otherwise this pivot is a huge mistake.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

Between President Trump’s decision to waive sanctions on Russia, his openness to a trilateral meeting with Russian President Putin and Chinese President Xi and the suspicious disruption of Starshield services in Ukraine, the White House is doing everything except saying out loud that it is turning on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky and the Ukrainian people. 

I think this is bad — full stop. I consider Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine not just an attack on a geopolitical ally but a moral affront, and I think abandoning Ukraine would be a strategic blunder. I see virtually nothing to gain from cozying up to Russia under the pretense that Putin will be amenable to peace negotiations if he’s given sanctions relief. 

Outside of the White House, these moves have little support. Writers on both sides, including many who typically back the administration, were nearly uniform in their opposition to the past week’s developments. The Trump-friendly New York Post editorial board (under “What the right is saying”) went so far as to invoke Neville Chamberlain regarding Trump’s openness to meeting with Putin and Xi. The closest thing we could find to a defense of Trump’s turn away from Ukraine was from Scott Pinsker at PJ Media (also under “What the right is saying”), who argued that Zelensky is motivated by ego and power. Pinsker didn’t explicitly defend Russia, but he essentially shrugged at Ukraine’s fate and said Trump has no obligation to care, either. 

If it were true that Ukraine was some tiny, irrelevant state whose fate meant nothing to the U.S., I could understand Pinsker’s sentiment, even if I still disagreed. But it isn’t true. 

The United States has much at stake in the outcome of the war in Ukraine. Start with the geopolitical implications: A Ukrainian surrender after the U.S. pulls its support would signal unwillingness to assist in future conflicts involving other allies (like, say, Taiwan). It would also call America’s broader credibility into question; if you’re a U.S. partner in the Middle East and see Trump abandon Ukraine just after starting a destabilizing war in your region, the incentive to maintain ties with the U.S. over Russia or China becomes much weaker. Relatedly, what message would it send to NATO allies? Could Finland, Poland, and the Baltic states trust that the U.S. would come to their defense against further Russian aggression?

Maybe you’re swayed by America First principles, and these possibilities in Europe don’t worry you. But even in terms of pure, selfish national interest, the U.S. still has much to gain from continuing to back Ukraine. The country’s pioneering development of drone technology makes it a powerful ally for current and future conflicts. As the writer Noah Smith said in May, “Ukraine’s intensive use of drones has allowed them to inflict casualty rates as high as 5 to 1 on the Russian army in recent months, while giving up little or no territory… In just the past year, Ukraine went from using just a few thousand [First-Person View] drones per day to using around 60,000.” In June, defense experts at the Council on Foreign Relations credited Ukraine’s drone strategy with reversing Russian territorial gains and “making it easier for Ukraine to sustainably defend itself.” 

To put the value of Ukraine’s military expertise in concrete terms: The U.S. is currently fighting a war with Iran, which is mimicking Russia’s drone strategy (high-volume deployments designed to overwhelm air defenses) to successfully target U.S. personnel and assets. Maintaining an alliance with Ukraine, a nation on the cutting edge of drone operations, provides both insights and direct, material support to the U.S. military in the Middle East. Ukraine’s expertise could prove exponentially more valuable to us in the long run than abandoning them to save some money or broker a lopsided peace deal.

Deep down, President Trump must understand the value Ukraine offers; just a few months ago, the countries signed a statement of intent for a new defense partnership focused on drone development, including exporting Ukrainian combat drones to the United States for military testing. What’s more, our continued support costs relatively little. As Rep. Dan Crenshaw (R-TX) noted this week, “Ukrainians have created the most efficient and lethal homegrown military industrial base in the world, one that can innovate and manufacture at the speed of the battlefield. The major backing Ukraine needs from the U.S. is intelligence and assistance with ballistic missile defense.” And while Trump bemoans the amount of military aid the U.S. has sent Ukraine, Congress hasn’t approved new spending on Ukraine since April 2024. Trump also neglects to mention the benefits from past appropriations, as Ukrainian contracts with U.S. manufacturers support American workers, suppliers, and defense production capacity. 

I’m not breaking any news here — we’ve known all of this for some time. So why the sudden change from the White House? The simplest explanation is that President Trump is trying to bring down energy prices ahead of the midterms, as he was with last week’s diesel deal. But just like that agreement, waiving sanctions on Russia is unlikely to meaningfully affect prices in the next two weeks, even if Ukraine scales back its strikes on Russian energy infrastructure. 

I also think Trump’s actions are personal. Zelensky is a wartime president who is constantly pushing for more support and resources and linking the West’s fate to Ukraine’s. I don’t blame him, but this posture is not the kind of diplomacy that Trump responds well to. Trump was clearly irritated by Zelensky’s refusal to pause strikes on Russian energy infrastructure (note: Russia hasn’t stopped its own strikes, either) after Trump’s unilateral push for a ceasefire. I suspect part of the motivation for the recent decisions is a desire to bring Zelensky to heel. 

It’s hard to know how much further Trump might push for a leadership change or whether he’s deploying the now-familiar move of ramping up pressure on an ally in pursuit of a larger goal. Either way, the Starshield slowdown speaks volumes. The blame game has quickly become convoluted here, but the latest reporting indicates that Elon Musk was the catalyst for the decision, with tacit support from Trump. Musk reportedly did this before — in the war’s first year — and now he and the president are playing an unconvincing game of pretending to have no idea who could be responsible for a directive only a handful of people on Earth could have given. Whoever is responsible, it’s cause for alarm in Ukraine, as the service is critical to supporting its aforementioned drone operations, and the slowdown forces their drones to fly blind over a certain speed. If the slowdown continues, the consequences for Ukraine could quickly spiral. 

As I said before, I think the U.S. has several reasons to continue supporting Ukraine, and I’m alarmed that the Trump administration apparently cannot appreciate them. But it’s too early to say outright that the U.S. has abandoned Ukraine or sided with Russia. Remember: The Trump–Zelensky relationship has looked beyond saving before, only for Trump to reverse course — as recently as July, he was praising Zelensky and giving his approval for Ukraine to build Patriot missiles (although that deal is now being held up). The president is fickle, and as difficult as that makes foreign relations, it also means he could reverse course. For now, I can only hope that Trump is engaging in gamesmanship and doesn’t go much further down this path. If he’s sincere, I hope influential voices in the administration can pull him back from the brink of irreversible moves. If the president’s vindictiveness and short-sighted politicking help Russia triumph in its detestable war, it will be a failure of the highest order.

Staff concurrence.
Ari Weitzman
Managing Editor
 
 
I want to zero in on one specific element of this story to demonstrate why the White House’s response to Ukraine’s Starshield outage is so gratuitously bad.
 
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is often cast in the role of “adult in the room,” had this to say on Saturday after Zelensky claimed their connectivity was restored but impaired: “Starshield is a contract with the U.S. military, it has nothing to do with Ukraine. I know Ukraine wants access to Starshield, they do not have Starshield now.”
 
Rubio’s current stance is to deny the White House’s involvement and stress that SpaceX’s decisions are their own. But out of the gate, his stance was to castigate Zelensky. “I’m not sure Zelensky knows what he’s talking about,” Rubio also said on Saturday.
 
But… Ukraine does have access to Starshield, and I’m pretty sure the Ukrainian president would know that. Why would Rubio deny this? I can only think of two options: Either he’s the one who doesn’t know what he’s talking about, meaning the administration’s most sober-minded foreign policy official is way off base, or Trump wanted to full-press a denial of this story and sacrificed Rubio’s credibility in the effort. I honestly don’t know which one’s worse, but both answers indicate a White House flailing in its foreign policy.

Take the survey: How will these recent developments impact the war? Let us know.

Disagree? That’s okay. Our opinion is just one of many. Write in and let us know why, and we’ll consider publishing your feedback.

item.title: The protests and riots in France.
item.dc:creator: Ari Weitzman
item.description: Plus, moonshine before the Supreme Court.
item.content:encoded:
Today’s topic.

The protests in France. For the past month, protests and riots have broken out across France, with violence and disorder significantly escalating over the weekend. In mid-September, high school students began demonstrating against a perceived lack of resources in schools; parents, college students, teachers and trade unions later joined the effort, and it has since broadened into nationwide unrest over cost-of-living concerns. French officials say that far-left groups are primarily responsible for the escalation into rioting and looting, while some French politicians and U.S. political leaders suggest the protests underscore deeper issues linked to immigration. 

Back up: The protests began in Paris-area schools, where students and parents have highlighted overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages, aging infrastructure, and a lack of investment in the education system. By early October, several violent incidents led to hundreds of arrests and dozens of injuries, as well as significant property damage. French officials claim that “ultra-left” groups, such as La France Insoumise, have catalyzed the violence and want to encourage chaos ahead of France’s 2027 elections. Right-wing politicians have argued that heightened levels of immigration and government tolerance of disorder have fueled the riots.

On Saturday, an estimated 550,000–800,000 protesters participated in 110 marches across France, and many demonstrations resulted in clashes between participants and police. Officials say approximately 1,000 law enforcement officers and firefighters were injured, 2,400 people were arrested, and 3,000 businesses were damaged. French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said police “had lost control” and suggested he would impose a national state of emergency if necessary. In a national address, French President Emmanuel Macron said, “Those who looted will have to pay back for the damage, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable.” Paris police issued a partial curfew Monday night. 

Some protesters have criticized the police response as overly aggressive, highlighting an incident where a 15-year-old student lost his hand from a police stun grenade. Many politicians, pundits and citizens have condemned the vandalism and rioting, though some protesters have defended it. “The state is violent and property damage is the people’s response to that violence,” one college student protester said. “The violence in the streets is against property, not people.” 

On Monday, President Donald Trump linked the riots to immigration, writing on Truth Social, “The migrants have taken over France. They must CLOSE THE BORDERS, FAST!” On X, Vice President JD Vance said, “Western liberals imported the third world into France and other countries in the name of diversity and compassion. They ignored fundamental questions of assimilation and compatibility. They were told it would lead to this and they didn’t listen.”

Today, we’ll have views from the left, right and French writers on the protests and riots, followed by Managing Editor Ari Weitzman’s take.

What the left is saying.
  • The left is mixed, with some suggesting the U.S. is similarly ripe for protest. 
  • Others question whether protests will address France’s underlying issues.

In The Philadelphia Inquirer, Will Bunch asked “do French protests have a message for America?”

“In recent years, billions of dollars in badly needed maintenance have been postponed, resulting in classrooms with toxic hazards like asbestos and ancient lead paint, stale, polluted air, inadequate heat in winter, and a lack of air-conditioning in summer,” Bunch wrote. “These, of course, are the K-12 conditions in the Philadelphia School District, and school squalor like this is something you see in a lot of large American cities, unfortunately.”

“But while there’s the occasional one-off rally… we’ve seen nothing when it comes to protesting like what’s happening this month in France,” Bunch said. “Unless you follow the big international news sites, the youth protests in France and India haven’t received extensive media coverage here in the U.S. You could argue that’s because we have plenty of our own problems on American soil… Which brings back the question: Why isn’t America’s Gen Z manning the barricades?”

The Economist argued “no one is addressing the core problems the country faces.”

“The context for the riots is the underlying tension linked to next year’s election… The country wants change, but is deeply divided about what should come next,” the writer said. “It looks probable that the polarisation of public debate and the politicisation of the street will intensify over the next six months — and probably beyond… [If Le Pen wins in 2027,] it could prompt a new round of protests on the left.”

“The government’s budget deficit is expected to be 5.4% of GDP this year, one of the highest in the euro zone,” the writer said. “Wariness in the markets and anger on the streets make for a toxic mix. Worse, as attention turns to law and order, France is even less likely to have the political conversation it badly needs: about what sort of welfare system it can afford and how to generate the wealth needed to sustain it.”

What the right is saying.
  • Some on the right worry ascendant ideologies in the U.S. could prompt similar protests. 
  • Others note the electoral factors affecting France’s protests.

In The Daily Signal, Steve Cortes said “Europe is burning — is America next?”

“A violent weekend of Marxist-Islamist protests rocked Europe, from Portugal to Italy. The worst carnage erupted across France, where rioters torched the revered, architecturally stunning town hall of Limoges. The 143-year-old landmark is a protected national monument. Its roof caved in, and its iconic bell tower collapsed into the flames,” Cortes wrote. “Is this kind of mayhem headed to America next?

“Sadly, current trends suggest that the growing ‘red-green’ alliance of hardcore leftists and radical Islamists in the United States could produce exactly this kind of disorder and destruction here, if we are not vigilant — and if the looming elections go poorly for nationalist candidates,” Cortes said. “Admittedly, [Marxist and Islamist] political factions make a strange political marriage, and they clearly disagree on many topics, especially social issues. So, what binds this dangerous new merger? A common enemy. They both hate Western civilization.”

The Wall Street Journal editorial board described “why France is burning.”

“The news this time is the pre-election play by far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon,” the board wrote. “The riots are ostensibly about declining public services, but the presidential election next April figures into the protest calculations… If the riots move more center-right voters away from the centrist candidates and toward Ms. Le Pen, Mr. Mélenchon may figure he has a fighting chance to become the next President in the May runoff.”

“The parties of the right and left see a rare opportunity to use the moment to gain the Élysée Palace,” the board said. “As a lame duck, [Macron] is left to rely on police to protect the French streets. They couldn’t do it on Saturday, as protesters ransacked shops in Marseille and elsewhere, and even torched the historic town hall in Limoges that survived the Nazis. France is in a violent democratic funk, and it will probably get worse. Don’t think it can’t happen in the U.S. given the current state of American politics.”

What writers in France are saying.
  • Some say the unrest is a response to President Macron’s failures.
  • Others criticize protesters for fomenting chaos.

The Le Monde editorial board said the protests “force Macron to confront the failures of his presidency.”

“Saturday’s protests should not be reduced to these acts of looting and destruction. French President Emmanuel Macron emphasized this in an address on Sunday evening,” the board wrote. “Yet, for the past 10 years, Macron has consistently turned a deaf ear to the social movements that have marked his two terms. Refusing compromise, his successive governments have systematically bypassed unions since 2017, contributing to their weakening. 

“By doing so, the authorities have deprived themselves of the essential intermediaries needed to channel public anger. Meanwhile, Macron has distanced himself from the youth by pushing unpopular reforms and ignoring their growing discontent,” the board said. “Listening to and respecting dialogue partners is essential. But above all, the government must give concrete political responses to their demands, which it can no longer afford to reject out of hand. Social peace can only be restored under these conditions.”

In The Free Press, Simone Rodan-Benzaquen called protesters’ actions “an assault on democracy.”

“The government needs to protect officials and teachers, prosecute their attackers, and get schools open. It needs to investigate police abuses seriously, without accepting that those abuses justify an assault on anyone in uniform,” Rodan-Benzaquen wrote. “I believe in the French Republic. I resent the suggestion that caring about its survival makes someone naive, or secretly authoritarian. We have the right to protest because we live in a democracy.

“We also have the right to go to school, to disagree with a crowd, and to elect a mayor who can do the job without fearing for his family,” Rodan-Benzaquen said. “Marseille’s city hall is not the Bastille. The people who broke into it were not staging a just revolution against authoritarianism; they were attacking the means by which their fellow citizens govern themselves… I want a government that understands how serious this is — and acts before another public servant, or another family, pays the price.”

My take.
Ari Weitzman
Managing Editor
 
 
  • The disorder in France is downstream of a few straightforward issues that have been building for some time.
  • More complicated factors are at play, too, prompting uncomfortable but necessary discussions about changes to French society.
  • Ultimately, France has a tough balance to strike between over-correction and not responding strongly enough.
Reminder: This is where we share a personal opinion. If you have feedback, criticism or compliments, leave a comment or reply to this email.

It’s tempting to tell a simple, three-part story about these protests and stop there.  

Part one of the simple story starts in the French suburb of Créteil, where students began protesting a lack of school resources. Protests are a fixture of French culture; as recently as 2018–2020, “Yellow Vest protesters” flooded the streets to demand the government address rising gas prices and weakening economic opportunities for workers.

A more recent fixture has been a forceful police response. In 2017, France passed a law allowing police to use weapons for reasons other than self-defense. Since then, French law enforcement has increased its use of non-lethal weapons against protesters, particularly guns that fire rubber pellets (called “lanceur de balles de défense,” or LBDs). Authorities said they needed to take stronger measures to respond to violent elements who commingle with protesters. 

Whatever the cause, the effect has been dramatic. Eye injuries caused by LBDs increased from two in 2016 and one in 2017 to 25 in 2018 and 15 in part of 2019. The sudden increase led to a rebuke from Europe’s human rights commissioner, who said France’s policing tactics against the Yellow Vest protesters were making it a violent outlier from the rest of Europe. 

That context is crucial to understanding part two, the tipping point that intensified the past month’s protests. In late September, the student-led protests spread from the Parisian suburbs to cities across France. On September 30, a 16-year-old was blinded in his right eye by injuries that prosecutors described as consistent with an LBD. Then, on October 5, a 15-year-old’s hand was blown off by a police grenade.

This incident ushered in part three, as at least 160,000 teachers and parents joined the marches. Protests spread across Europe. The Yellow Vests joined the movement. Then, rioting and looting broke out in French cities over the weekend — rioters burned a tourist office in Lyon, set fire to the 143-year-old town hall in Limoges, and looted Marseille’s city center. By Monday morning, at least 3,000 storefronts had been vandalized, and looters in Marseille were brazenly gathering their spoils in broad daylight.

In the simple story, a protest about something specific began attracting dissatisfied factions, particularly from the left, who were more bent on destruction and crime than delivering a political message (and who actually undermined the original message the students were raising). But that narrative doesn’t tell the whole story. Instead, the whole story asks you to confront an uncomfortable element that is easy to discern the moment you start watching videos, listening to eyewitnesses, or reading local accounts.

Right-wing commenter Thaïs d’Escufon presented this element as strongly as possible in two contrasting videos. In the first, a white woman is pleading with the mob not to loot a nearby store, saying “this isn’t for the cause” as she is gently held back by a member of the crowd. In the second, a Muslim business owner trying to protect her storefront is aided by members of the crowd, who tell looters “don’t smash it up, she’s a sister” and “it’s okay, my brothers, please go.”

As French writer Charles Consigny bluntly stated on a daily French talk show, “the looters are children of immigrants.” Frankly, I’m having a hard time processing that claim — because I’m finding more reason to support it than to reject it. On the same show, a caller who identified herself as a Muslim business owner whose shop had been looted in Marseille said, “It’s unfortunate, but 80% — it’s my community.” Additionally, a police union representative said most of the looters were from “disadvantaged neighborhoods,” outlying communities like Créteil that are often home to immigrant families.

Conversely, the response that Green Party MP Sandrine Rousseau gave to Consigny was a passionate plea not to blame immigrants for the damage, saying immigrants are part of the fabric of French culture and many are firefighters and police responding to the destruction. Rousseau is right, almost obviously so: Most immigrant families are law-abiding citizens who contribute to the societies of their adopted home countries. However, Rousseau notably didn’t deny Consigny’s central claim, which is somewhat telling. I’m not willing to go as far as to say that the rioting in Marseille is proof of “migrant chaos” causing “Europe’s decline,” but as of this moment, I have more reason to believe Consigny than I do to dismiss him. So, if it’s true that many of the looters were children of immigrants, why is that the case?

I think that question has a scary answer that I’m hesitant to agree with and an easy answer that doesn’t tell us much. The hard answer is what Steve Cortes wrote in The Daily Signal (under “What the right is saying”), that these looters are representative of a tide of migrants who hate Western civilization but are increasingly seeking refuge in Western civilization. The easy answer is simply that the rioters and looters come from poor families, who tend to disproportionately be immigrant families, and their rioting and looting is largely an economic impulse. 

Grappling with these answers is very uncomfortable and difficult for me. I generally tend towards accepting the easy answer, but I’m aware of how, well, easy it is. I also don’t think the civilizational concern should just be dismissed out of hand, especially as French social media is awash with videos reposting a 1979 speech by Ayatollah Khomeini over images of rioting and destruction in France from this past weekend. The ‘red–green’ alliance between communist protesters and Islamist extremists that Cortes described feels meaningful to me, as does the paucity of the responses to this criticism from the left. 

Frankly, I don’t know how anyone can deny that the communist/Islamist rhetoric coming from these protesters is oppositional towards Western civilization. However, I have a much harder time accepting that young students calling themselves communists or online posters calling for an anti-Western jihad are the same people smashing up a Hermès store to sell handbags online. I’ve spent plenty of time on college campuses — the people espousing the most extreme rhetoric are often not at all willing to back it up with correspondingly extreme actions, instead opting for more milquetoast public disruptions. I ultimately believe that the worst of the weekend’s riots came from low-brow opportunists, the same kind of people who look for excuses to steal, smash and burn that we’ve seen time and time again, in the U.S. and abroad.

France is now tasked with drawing a line between protecting its long-practiced ability to demonstrate publicly and punishing crimes committed during those demonstrations. As of today, it’s pushing back against the resale of stolen goods and instigating curfews, while politicians from the left are themselves pushing back against the crackdown as collective punishment. If France goes too far in its enforcement, it risks its own culture of protests and citizen trust in the government. But if it doesn’t go far enough, it will not only send a permissive signal to opportunists who came out under the cover of protests, but to the red–green alliance itself. It’s a delicate moment, and if the French government gets this wrong, the circumstances could be dire and long-lasting.

Staff dissent.
Audrey Moorehead
Editor
 
 
I understand Ari’s desire to differentiate between online agitators whose rhetoric doesn’t translate into action and the opportunists who use civil unrest as an excuse to loot and burn, but I ultimately find it misguided.
 
Ideological opposition to the West is an ever-present problem in France, Europe at large, and even the United States. Some of this opposition is homegrown, coming from lifelong Westerners who have become enraptured with visions of a secular, utopian communist future (usually leftist agitators) or with romanticizations of a white Christian pastoral age gone by (usually rightist agitators). But some of this radicalism is brought in from elsewhere, by immigrants who seek the economic opportunities of the West without embracing the culture that produced those opportunities.
 
And to Ari’s point, most of these agitators are just blowhards; X’s Nazi propagandists and Bluesky’s Mao apologists are not necessarily the ones throwing bricks through store windows. But the normalization of opposition to the West creates the conditions for violence: It motivates people to look the other way from looting and burning, or even to permit looting and burning in service of broader goals. So while these French protests aren’t going to be the killing blow that starts the revolution, they’re another brick through a window of Western civilization; and the people inside the building are becoming less and less likely to want to patch it up.
 
If we admit that we must combat anti-Western radicalism, we have to think about how to do it. Combating homegrown radicalism, which is usually borne out of misunderstandings of the Western tradition, is difficult — it requires being more intentional about presenting the tradition’s past and its desired future. But combating imported radicalism has an easier solution: It requires revisiting immigration policies and examining whether a stopper on immigration, in order to better assimilate extant migrant populations, might be useful.
